system_overview: This specification models the BOSCO (Byzantine One-Step COnsensus) algorithm from Song and van Renesse's 2008 paper. BOSCO is a one-step Byzantine asynchronous consensus protocol that allows processes to decide in a single communication round under favorable conditions. When a one-step decision is not possible, processes fall back to an underlying consensus protocol. The algorithm tolerates up to T Byzantine faults among N processes, requiring N greater than 3T.
actors_and_components: The system consists of N processes. The last F processes (where F is at most T) are designated as faulty (Byzantine) and may send arbitrary messages, including voting for both values simultaneously. The remaining N-F processes are correct and follow the protocol. Byzantine processes are not modeled with explicit actions; their influence is captured through the message-receiving mechanism that allows correct processes to receive arbitrary messages attributed to faulty senders.
state_variables: The system tracks: the control location of each correct process (representing its current phase: initial proposal of 0 or 1, sent vote for 0 or 1, decided on 0 or 1, or deferred to underlying consensus with value 0 or 1), the set of messages sent by correct processes (pairs of sender and vote type), and the set of messages received by each correct process.
initial_state: Initially, no messages have been sent and no messages have been received. Each correct process starts with a proposed value, either 0 or 1, chosen nondeterministically.
actions: The protocol proceeds as follows: (1) Each process receives a set of messages that may include messages from both correct and Byzantine senders. (2) A process that proposed 0 broadcasts a vote for 0 and moves to the sent-0 state. Similarly, a process that proposed 1 broadcasts a vote for 1 and moves to the sent-1 state. (3) After sending, a process waits until it has received messages from at least N-T distinct senders. Then: (a) If it received more than (N+3T)/2 votes for value 0, it decides 0 in one step. (b) If it received more than (N+3T)/2 votes for value 1, it decides 1 in one step. (c) If it received more than (N-T)/2 votes for 0 and fewer than (N-T)/2 votes for 1, it defers to the underlying consensus with value 0 (and similarly with the values swapped). (d) If neither value has a clear majority (both have at least (N-T)/2 votes), the process defers to underlying consensus with its own originally proposed value. One-step decisions have priority over fallback to underlying consensus.
safety_properties: Lemma 3 (agreement on one-step decisions): if any correct process decides 0 in one step, no correct process decides 1 in one step, and vice versa. Lemma 4 (consistency between one-step and underlying): if any correct process decides 0 in one step, no correct process defers to underlying consensus with value 1, and vice versa. OneStep0: if all correct processes propose 0, then no correct process decides 1, defers with value 0, or defers with value 1. OneStep1: if all correct processes propose 1, then no correct process decides 0, defers with value 0, or defers with value 1.
model_bounds: For model checking: N=4, T=1, F=1. The process set is 1 through N. Correct processes are 1 through N-F, and faulty processes are N-F+1 through N. Two auxiliary parameters are computed: more than (N+3T)/2 and more than (N-T)/2, using integer division with ceiling.
additional_assumptions: The specification does not include fairness conditions; it uses only the safety part of the temporal specification. The one-step decision thresholds have strict priority: a process checks the stronger one-step conditions before the weaker underlying-consensus conditions. If N is greater than 7T, the OneStep0 and OneStep1 properties hold; they do not hold otherwise. The model requires N greater than 3T, T at least F, and F at least 0.
